1:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the shape of the whole chapter: two long registers, the first of the valiant men who went over to David before Saul died, the second of the fighting men who anointed him king in Hebron. The first they divide again into three — the Benjamites who reached him during his stay in Ziklag, the Gadites and the men of Judah and Benjamin who found him in the mountain fastnesses, and the Manassites who joined him as he returned to Ziklag before Saul's last battle.

Ziklag is given a history. Keil and Delitzsch trace it to Joshua's allotment to the Simeonites (Joshua 19:5; 1 Chronicles 4:30), which later passed into Philistine possession; Ellicott places it within the territory of Judah but assigned to Simeon, seized by the Philistines, then given by Achish of Gath to David, whose headquarters it remained for sixteen months until the death of Saul. Gill and Clarke put the gift plainly — Achish gave it him to live in when he fled, a safe retreat from Saul's wrath.

The clause that David "yet kept himself close" is where Ellicott finds the Hebrew concise and obscure, though he judges the Authorised Version to render it fairly: David was still shut up in his stronghold, or restrained within bounds, out of dread of King Saul — or the sense may be that he was banished from Saul's presence. Henry turns the same clause into the point of the paragraph. David did not appear, and so did not encourage his well-wishers to come in, not foreseeing that Saul's death was so near; and yet while he kept close God was inclining and preparing them to come over with seasonable succours. All the force he had while he was persecuted was six hundred men who served for his guards; when he must begin to act offensively, Providence brought in more. Those who trust God to do his work in his own way and time, Henry concludes, find his providence outdoing all their forecast and contrivance. "Helpers of the war" Ellicott reads as helpers in war, allies or companions in arms, the men who made the forays against Geshur, Gezer and Amalek (1 Samuel 27:8).

On the armament the comment turns technical. Gill notes only that bows were much used in war in those times. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the Hebrew as "those preparing bows," men armed with bows, matching a synonymous phrase elsewhere in the book (1 Chronicles 8:40; compare 2 Chronicles 17:17; Psalms 78:9), and then "with the right and left hand practised upon stones," to hurl them, "and in arrows on the bow," to shoot therewith. Ellicott translates "drawers of the bow" and calls the men ambidextrous, adding that the left-handed slingers of Benjamin were famous from of old (Judges 20:16) — the verse Henry reaches for too, writing that they were trained up in shooting and slinging and used both hands alike, ingenious active men of whom a few might much serve David.

What moved them is not stated, and two answers are offered. Henry admits we are not told, and guesses at a generous indignation at the base treatment Saul had given David, which would animate them to appear the more vigorously for him, that the guilt and reproach of it might not lie upon them. Wesley looks past motive of that kind to God's Spirit, which moved them, together with the conscience of their duty to David and their observation that God had departed from Saul and was specially present with David. The phrase "of Saul's brethren" Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both read narrowly: it means the men of his tribe, not his nearer relatives, and "of Benjamin" is added to make clear that his immediate kinsmen are not intended.
3:
The list opens with a title rather than a name. Ellicott renders "the chief" as captain of the band, the Hebrew word being simply "head"; Keil and Delitzsch take it the same way, the leader of this host of warriors. Gill reads the two at its head, Ahiezer and Joash, as sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite, which Ellicott vocalises from the Hebrew as Hashshemaah.

Much of what follows is topography. The Gibeathite belongs to Gibeah of Saul, which Ellicott locates between Ramah and Anathoth (Isaiah 10:29) and which also goes by the name Gibeah of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 11:31; Judges 20:4); Keil and Delitzsch send the reader to Joshua's account of its situation. Gill draws the consequence the register leaves implicit — Gibeah was Saul's birthplace, so these men might be some of his kindred. Jehu the Antothite comes from Anathoth, a priests' city, now Anata. Azmaveth, Ellicott suggests, may be the warrior of Bahurim named among David's heroes (1 Chronicles 11:33), and Jeziel is the Hebrew margin's form where the text reads Jezuel, a variation he sets beside Peniel and Penuel.

Ishmaiah the Gibeonite draws the longest note. Gill makes him a man of Gibeon, another city in the tribe of Benjamin, who came with a command of his own. Ellicott argues the point from the register itself: Gibeon belonged to Benjamin (1 Chronicles 9:35), and because the whole company is described as of Saul's brethren of Benjamin, Ishmaiah was a Benjamite rather than a Gibeonite in the strict sense of the term. The "thirty" among whom he was mighty Ellicott identifies with the famous corps (1 Chronicles 11:25), and he accounts for the absence of Ishmaiah's name from that catalogue by supposing he died before it was drawn up.

What "over the thirty" adds is disputed. Ellicott offers two possibilities and settles on neither — that at one time Ishmaiah was captain of the band, or that the phrase is merely comparative, marking him a hero above the thirty. Wesley reads it instead as a detail of the man's arrival: he came attended with thirty valiant Benjamites, and was their commander.

The remaining names are handled by etymology. Jerimoth Ellicott recognises as a Benjamite name; Bealiah he reads as "Baal is Jah," and takes names of that make as evidence that Baal was once a title of the God of Israel. The Haruphite is a patronymic, which Keil and Delitzsch explain as denoting either a descendant of Haruph or a member of the children of Hariph whom Nehemiah's register lists alongside the Gibeonites — Ellicott notices the same juxtaposition, the sons of Hariph standing just before the sons of Gibeon. Gill is content to call the man a native of Haruph or Hariph, and the Hebrew margin here reads Hariphite. Josabad the Gederathite Ellicott places at Gederah in the lowland of Judah (Joshua 15:36), and wonders whether he is the Zabad named in the roll of the thirty (1 Chronicles 11:41).
6:
Five names close the Benjamite roll — Elkanah, Jesiah, Azareel, Joezer and Jashobeam — and who the Korhites among whom they are counted were is the one real quarrel in these verses. Keil and Delitzsch hold without doubt that they were descendants of the Levite Korah, one division of whom David afterwards made guardian of the thresholds of the tent he erected for the ark on Zion, because their fathers had held the office of watchers at the entrance of the camp of the LORD (1 Chronicles 9:18). Elkanah and Azareel they call thoroughly Levitic names, and they suggest that service in the porter's office in the holy place may have roused the desire that brought these men out to David. Gill denies the identification outright: these are not the Korahites descended from Levi but the posterity of a Korah of Benjamin.

Ellicott begins where Keil and Delitzsch do, counting five members of the Levitical clan Korah and observing that Elkanah occurs three times in the line of Heman the Korhite musician and again in Samuel's (1 Chronicles 6:33; 1 Chronicles 6:22), that Azareel is a priestly name (Nehemiah 11:13), and that there must have been Levites about the tabernacle at Gibeon. But he leaves a third possibility open, that these men belonged to the Judean clan Korah (1 Chronicles 2:43), otherwise unknown. Jesiah he vocalises Yishshiyahu and glosses "Jahu is my possession" (Psalms 16:5), and he notes that a Jashobeam has already stood at the head of the three heroes (1 Chronicles 11:11).

The last pair, Joelah and Zebadiah, sons of Jeroham of Gedor, raise a difficulty of another kind, since the names look Judaean in a list of Benjamites. Gill registers it without resolving it: Gedor was a city in the tribe of Judah and might now belong to Benjamin, or else this was another city of the same name in that tribe. Ellicott sets out the evidence on both sides. Jeroham is the name of a Benjamite clan and two Benjamite chiefs bear the name Zebadiah (1 Chronicles 8:27; 1 Chronicles 8:15); on the other hand Gedor was a town of Judah, south-west of Bethlehem (1 Chronicles 4:4). He reports the explanation some give, that the chronicler has welded two lists into one, and prefers a simpler account: towns did not always stay in the hands of the tribes to which they were first assigned, and some Judaean towns may have held a partly Benjaminite population.

Keil and Delitzsch use the clause that follows to open the second of their three sub-registers, and in doing so they date it. David's sojourn in the mountain hold falls in the first years of his flight from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1), and the word for the hold, pointed here so as to bind it closely to what comes after, is the same in sense as the term used of his stronghold elsewhere (1 Samuel 24:22). The addition "to the wilderness" shows that a mountain top or mountain fortress in the wilderness of Judah is meant; and comparing the narrative of those years they conclude that David did not then hide in one single fixed place.
8:
The verb the register uses is "separated themselves," and each voice supplies what it was from. Gill has them leaving the rest of their tribe, their families and dwellings, and the government of Saul. Ellicott puts it more pointedly: they separated from the royalists of Gad, who clung to Saul. Henry, reading them as men convinced of David's title to the government and his fitness for it, calls the act a laudable separation, made though David was in the hold in the wilderness; and he counts what it was worth, since they were but few, eleven in all, yet added much to David's strength. Most of the earlier recruits, Henry adds, had been men of broken fortunes, distressed and discontented, soldiers of fortune who came for protection rather than to do David service (1 Samuel 22:2), whereas these were men of war and fit for the battle.

Where the hold stood nobody will say for certain. Gill offers a strong hold in the wilderness of Ziph or Maon, or, as some think, Ziklag, the hold there being said to lie in the wilderness of Judah. Ellicott lists the candidates — perhaps the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1), or the wooded mount of Hachilah (1 Samuel 23:19), or the crag of Maon, or the rocks of En-gedi (1 Samuel 23:25) — and observes that caves and holds are named together as refuges (Judges 6:2), David in the earlier period of his outlawry taking shelter in the natural fastnesses of Judaea. Henry's guess falls on En-gedi as well.

The description itself Ellicott takes apart term by term. "Men of might" is the phrase used elsewhere of mighty men of valour (1 Chronicles 5:24; 1 Chronicles 7:2); "men of war fit for the battle" is literally men of service or training, that is, veterans; and what they handled was shield and spear, buckler being the reading of some old editions against the manuscripts, which have the word for a lance (compare Jeremiah 46:3). The lion-faced clause he sets out as verse — "And face of the lion, their face; And like gazelles on the mountains they speed" — and the poetic style, he says, betrays an ancient source from which the chronicler is clearly borrowing, much as David's own lament over Saul and Jonathan is poetry of the same cast (2 Samuel 1:23) and the title Ariel, lion of God, serves for a champion (1 Chronicles 11:22; Isaiah 29:1). For the swiftness he points to what is said of Asahel (2 Samuel 2:18).

That swiftness holds Clarke and Henry both. Clarke notes that speed was reckoned a grand accomplishment in a warrior, as appears from all the ancient writings which treat of military affairs; Henry turns it to the men's use, calling them of incredible swiftness not to fly from the enemy but to fly upon him and pursue his scattered forces, so that none could escape them — while their lions' faces meant none could out-fight them. Their discipline he counts as a second thing: trained up to military exercises, able to use both offensive and defensive weapons.

Gill gives the eleven in order — Ezer first, then Obadiah, Eliab, Mishmannah, Jeremiah, Attai, Eliel, Johanan, Elzabad, a second Jeremiah, Machbanai — and allows that the order may follow age, or merit, or the sequence in which they came to David. Ellicott glosses "the first" simply as the chief, and Keil and Delitzsch read the subscription that follows them as marking chief warriors rather than leaders of the host.
14:
The subscription that closes the Gadite list — "these were of the sons of Gad, captains of the host" — Ellicott marks as a subscription and renders literally as heads of the host, chief warriors; Keil and Delitzsch press the same distinction, chief warriors rather than leaders of the army. Gill reads the title as an office held at home: they were captains of the militia in their own country, and of the men they brought with them, or else became such afterwards in David's army. Henry makes the point practically — they were officers of the militia in their own tribe, so that although they did not bring soldiers with them, they had hundreds and thousands at command.

The clause about the hundred and the thousand is the one place in the register where the translations part company. The text as it stands makes the least of them an officer over a hundred and the greatest over a thousand, which is the rendering Ellicott credits to the Syriac and the Vulgate; but he judges the margin correct, and reads the Hebrew as "One to a hundred, the little one; and the great one to a thousand," noting that David's band at this time was only about six hundred strong, and that the phrasing is poetic, or at least rhetorical, and quite unlike the chronicler's usual style. Keil and Delitzsch argue it on grammar. The sense must be that the weaker of them could cope with a hundred men and the stronger with a thousand — a reading they call the only correct one and credit to Bertheau and the older Jewish commentators — while the Vulgate's version is inadmissible, since it would have required a different preposition in the Hebrew. Keil and Delitzsch anchor the sense on one cross-reference, Ellicott on two (Leviticus 26:8; Deuteronomy 32:30).

The crossing of Jordan is taken by all of them as evidence of courage. Gill notes only that they had to come over the river to reach David, since they dwelt on the other side, and names the month Nisan or Ab. Clarke takes the first month for Nisan, answering to part of our March and April, and offers two ways of reading the timing: this was probably before the snows on the mountains were melted, just as Jordan began to overflow its banks, or, if the river had already overflowed, the attempt was the more hazardous and the proof of their heroism the greater. Ellicott drives at the same conclusion — they did not wait till summer had made the Jordan shallow, but crossed in spring when it was perilously swollen with the rains and the melted snows of Lebanon (compare Joshua 3:15), the verb meaning that the river was filling or brimming over. Henry has them swim it, and draws the lesson that those are fit to be employed in the cause of God who can venture so in dependence upon the divine protection.

What they did on the far bank closes the paragraph. Ellicott translates "they made all the valleys flee," understanding the inhabitants, who were hostile to the enterprise, and takes the two directions as toward the sunrise and the sunset, or on both sides of the river. Henry admits that who those enemies were does not appear, but has the Gadites put them to flight with their lion-like faces and pursue them with matchless fury, which way soever they turned following their blow and not doing their work by halves.
16:
Two tribes arrive without names. Gill marks the men of Benjamin and Judah as a company besides those already listed, and Keil and Delitzsch notice the omission and account for it — their names are not in the lists, possibly because they were not handed down in the historical works the chronicler used. Ellicott sends the reader back to the hold already described.

Why David came out to them is read two ways, and Gill holds both open: either out of respect and deference, some of them being persons of eminence, or out of suspicion, since they were chiefly of the tribe of Benjamin and he wanted to sound them before admitting them. Henry has no doubt it was the second. David was surprised to see them and could not but conceive some jealousy of their intentions, having so often been endangered by the treachery of the men of Ziph and the men of Keilah, who were themselves all men of Judah; a man whose life was so struck at might well be timorous, and one so often deceived might well be suspicious. Ellicott keeps to the wording: David went out from his fastness or hiding-place in the hill or wood, literally before them, that is, he confronted them. Both David's speech and Amasai's answer, he adds, have all the marks of a genuine survival of antiquity.

The terms David sets out Ellicott glosses clause by clause. "If for peace ye have come unto me to help me" uses peace for friendly intent (Psalms 120:7), and "to help me" picks up the description of his comrades as helpers of the war. "Mine heart shall be knit unto you" is literally that he will have toward them a heart for union, a heart at one with them and true to them — the same oneness of heart the chapter ends with (Psalms 133:1). The alternative is literally to beguile him for his foes, that is, to betray him to them, and for that treachery Ellicott reaches back to Sextus Tarquinius at Gabii and Zopyrus at Babylon. "Seeing there is no wrong in mine hands" is "although there be no violence in my palms" (Job 16:17; Isaiah 53:9), and the closing verbs are jussive or optative (2 Chronicles 24:22) — the psalms breathing throughout a confidence that the LORD is a righteous judge who never fails to vindicate innocence and punish high-handed violence and treacherous cunning (Psalms 9:12).

Henry reads the speech as fair dealing: as they are, they shall find him. If they are faithful he will be their rewarder, thankfully accepting their good-will though they come late and bring no great strength; if they come to betray him into Saul's hands under colour of friendship, he leaves them to God to be their avenger. He will not be judge in his own cause, though a wise man, nor avenge himself, though a man of valour. He imprecates no fearful judgement, but refers his cause modestly to the divine wisdom and justice, asking only that the LORD look upon it and rebuke it — for it becomes those who appeal to God, Henry says, to express themselves with great temper and moderation.

On "the God of our fathers" Wesley and Henry say much the same. The title covers both his fathers and theirs, reminding them not to deal ill with him, since both descend from the same patriarchs and serve the same God; and it encourages David to believe that God would right him if he were abused, as the God of his fathers and a God to all Israel as well as Judge of all the earth.
18:
The verb here is vivid, and the renderings differ. Gill translates "clothed," a spirit of fortitude — as the Targum has it — of strength, courage and presence of mind, with which Amasai was endowed, covered and clothed as with a garment. Clarke gives the Targum's paraphrase whole: the spirit of fortitude clothed Amasai, chief of the mighty men, and he answered, "For thy sake, O David, are we come, that we may be with thee, thou son of Jesse." The Syriac, Ellicott reports, has the spirit of valour.

Whose Spirit it was the others settle. Keil and Delitzsch take the Spirit of God to be meant, the divine name omitted only because all that mattered was to show that Amasai's resolution was the effect of a higher spiritual influence (compare Judges 6:34; 2 Chronicles 24:20). Ellicott thinks the word for God has probably fallen out of the Hebrew, and presses the point: we may prefer to say that Amasai spoke under a sudden impulse of enthusiasm, but if we look deeper and seek a definite interpretation of our terms we shall allow that the impulses of spirit are spiritual, and that enthusiasm for truth and right is indeed a sort of divine possession — the Spirit of the LORD being the source of true courage as of all other spiritual gifts (Isaiah 11:2). Henry is careful to say it was no spirit of prophecy but one of wisdom and resolution suited to the occasion, putting unpremeditated words into his mouth proper both to satisfy David and to animate those who came with him. Wesley makes the general point: not only saving graces but other heroical and generous motions are ascribed to God's Spirit, which here stirred in Amasai a more than ordinary greatness of mind.

Who Amasai was nobody states flatly. Gill calls him a sister's son of David's. Ellicott thinks him perhaps the Amasa son of Abigail whom Joab murdered out of jealousy (1 Chronicles 2:17; 2 Samuel 20:10). Keil and Delitzsch report the same conjecture from the older commentators, noting that the name appears nowhere else in David's history although the man must have held a very important position. Henry leaves it open: whether he is the Amasa who afterwards sided with Absalom does not appear. His title is disputed too: the Hebrew text makes him head of the Thirty, the Greek, Syriac and Latin agreeing, and Ellicott judges the margin's "knights" or chariot-soldiers less probable, adding that since Amasai is absent from the catalogue of the Thirty he is called their chief here by anticipation.

The answer itself Ellicott prints as verse — "To thee, David! And with thee, son of Ishai! Peace, peace to thee. And peace to thine helper; For thy God hath holpen thee!" — and reads it as a direct reply to David's question: they will be fast friends with him and with all who befriend him, because God is on his side. Henry hears in "son of Jesse" a title Saul had used in disdain but these men took for David's honour, reminding themselves that he was lineally descended from Nahshon and Salmon, princes of Judah in their day; and the peace they wished, he notes, was no drinking of healths but a prayer. It is good, Henry adds, if we must side, to side with those that side with God and have God with them.

David's acceptance closes the verse. Ellicott marks the late Hebrew word for "received," the chronicler resuming his own narrative, and renders the last clause as bestowing them among the heads of the band — officers of a little army continually growing by such adhesions (1 Samuel 22:2). Henry draws the manners out: charity and honour teach us to let fall our jealousies as soon as satisfaction is given us.
19:
The verb "there fell" is a technical one. Ellicott calls it the regular term for desertion of one cause for another (2 Kings 25:11), and Keil and Delitzsch say the same — to fall to someone is used specially of deserters in war who leave their lord and go over to the enemy (1 Samuel 29:3). Gill keeps it plain: men of the tribe of Manasseh took David's part and joined him.

The circumstance is the awkward one of David in the Philistine host. Keil and Delitzsch set it out: the Manassites came over when David marched with the Philistines against Israel and yet did not help them, because upon advisement the lords of the Philistines sent him away, saying that at the price of their own heads he would fall away to his master Saul. The narrative in Samuel, they add, is the historical commentary on the event, for when the Philistine lords gathered their forces against Saul, David, who had found refuge with Achish, was compelled to join their host (1 Samuel 29:2). Henry reads the same awkwardness as providence: the opportunity was given these men when David and his company marched through their country, Achish having taken David out with him to fight against Saul until the lords of the Philistines obliged him to withdraw (1 Samuel 29:4). Ellicott treats the verse as a summary of that whole stretch of the story, down to the sack of Ziklag.

Two phrases in it draw closer attention. "Upon advisement" is after deliberation (Proverbs 20:18), a cross-reference Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both reach for; "to the jeopardy of our heads" Ellicott renders at the price of our heads (1 Chronicles 11:19), glossing the Philistine calculation as the fear that by betraying them David would make his peace with his old master. On "they helped them not" Ellicott takes the subject to be David and his men, who did not help the Philistines, but raises the possibility that the right reading is "he helped them" rather than "they helped them."

The second company came later. Gill distinguishes them from the first — these joined David when he had been dismissed from the Philistines and was returning to Ziklag — and Wesley says as much in a line. Ellicott dates the meeting: on his dismissal by the Philistine princes David went back with his men to Ziklag (1 Samuel 30:1), and on the way the Manassite chieftains joined him, probably before the battle that decided the fate of Saul and his sons (1 Samuel 29:11).

Two details of the list itself remain. The name Jozabad stands twice, which Ellicott thinks may be a scribe's error, comparing the doubled Jeremiah in the Gadite roll earlier in the chapter. And the title "captains of the thousands that were of Manasseh" he connects with the interchange of "thousand" and "father-house" (Numbers 31:14; 1 Chronicles 13:1), suggesting that each clan may originally have furnished a thousand warriors to the tribal host.
21:
The band David was helped against is usually read as the Amalekites. Gill names them outright — while David was away with the Philistines they had seized Ziklag and burnt it and carried the women captive, and these men coming so opportunely assisted him in the pursuit. Wesley says the same in a line, and Henry adds that the Manassites were not many but were all mighty men and did David good service on that occasion. Ellicott reports that the Vulgate and Syriac read it so too, and that the explanation has been sought where the Amalekite band is spoken of (1 Samuel 30:8). But the Hebrew text of the clause has been called "brief and unintelligible", and he proposes another rendering: "And these helped David over the band," that is, in the joint command of his forces, as the previous verse had made Amasai's company captains of the band. It is pretty clear, he argues, that the names so far are those of captains and chiefs rather than ordinary warriors, and that these two verses form a subscription to the list.

Who "they" are is disputed on grammatical grounds. Keil and Delitzsch take the pronoun for the Manassites just named, matching the way the same construction opens the chapter. Bertheau, whom they report, refers it instead to all the heroes from the first verse onward, on two grounds: that the Manassites were not alone in the conflict with Amalek, since David won that victory with his whole force of six hundred men (1 Samuel 30:9), among whom those already named must be included; and that the chapter distinguishes clearly between the men who came in at an earlier period and those who came later.

The closing summary reads as a daily accumulation. Gill dates it particularly after Saul's defeat by the Philistines, down to the time David came to Hebron; Wesley spreads it over the stay at Ziklag, the march to Hebron, and chiefly Hebron itself. Ellicott translates "For at the time of each day men used to come to David to help him, amounting to a mighty camp, like a camp of God," and says the verse explains why David needed so many captains and why his troop is called an army. Henry turns it into providence: David's interest grew strangely just when he had occasion to make use of it, auxiliary forces flocking in daily till he had a great host — and when the promise comes to the birth, Henry says, leave it to God to find strength to bring it forth.

What "like the host of God" means is the phrase everybody weighs. Ellicott hears an antique colouring in it and sets it beside Jacob's word at Mahanaim, where the angels of God met him and he called the place God's camp (Genesis 32:1; Joshua 13:30); ancient Hebrew, he observes, denotes excellence by reference to the divine standard, as in the hills of God and the cedars of God (Psalms 36:6; Psalms 80:11). Keil and Delitzsch reach for those same phrases but argue against reading numbers into it: the host is one God has formed and in which his power shows itself, and its greatness is to be estimated by power and spirit rather than by the count of warriors — against Movers' charge of an idealizing historian they point out that David had at first four hundred and afterwards six hundred valiant men, against whom Saul with his thousands could accomplish nothing. Clarke's Targum goes the other way, glossing it as a very numerous army, like the army of the angel of God, and Wesley likewise takes it for innumerable, like the stars or the angels, both of which are called God's hosts. Ellicott adds that the verse seems to take in the accessions that followed Saul's death.
23:
With this verse the register changes its subject, and Henry marks the change: what follows is an account of those who were active in perfecting the settlement of David upon the throne after the death of Ishbosheth, when all the tribes came to Hebron, either themselves or by their representatives, to make him king — and what the chronicler gives is the quota each tribe brought in ready armed, in case there should be any opposition. Clarke dates it to the same point, after the death of Ish-bosheth, Saul's son (2 Samuel 4:5). Gill glosses the armed bands as men trained up to war and accounted fit for it.

The heading's key word divides the versions. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the Vulgate's "chiefs of the army" and take the term literally for sums — that is, companies or bands of soldiers, the sense they find for it in Judges and Samuel (Judges 7:16; 1 Samuel 11:1) — while allowing that it might also stand for heads in the sense of individuals (Judges 5:30). Both meanings, they say, are linguistically certain, so Bertheau cannot claim that the well-ascertained use of language settles it for leaders of the army, nor that another word would have been used had the chronicler meant to count by heads. Ellicott lays out the same two options and prefers "totals" or "bands," noting that the usual word for a poll is "skull"; and he adds an argument from the list itself — the Vulgate and the Greek render "chiefs of the army," but no chiefs are named in it except those of the Aaronites, and one ambiguous term in a heading cannot be allowed to alter the character of the whole. The Syriac, he observes, omits the verse altogether. The word for the equipped men Keil and Delitzsch call a collective noun denoting the equipped manhood.

Three further phrases are glossed. Ellicott notes that the conjunction before "came to David" is wanting in the Hebrew, so that "they came to David at Hebron" reads as a parenthesis unless a relative has dropped out. "To turn the kingdom" is literally to bring it round out of the direct line of natural heredity (1 Chronicles 10:14). And "according to the word" is literally according to the mouth (1 Chronicles 11:3) — what the LORD had spoken by Samuel being virtually the word of his own mouth.

Judah's contingent of six thousand eight hundred raises the question that governs the whole list. Ellicott notices the order of march, which proceeds from south to north and then crosses to the tribes beyond Jordan, and accounts for Judah's modest figure by the seven years in which that tribe had already acknowledged David's sovereignty: it had no need to appear in full force at his recognition by the others. Wesley says the men came in the name of their brethren, for that whole tribe stuck to David. Henry generalises the pattern — the tribes that lived nearest brought the fewest, Judah six thousand eight hundred and Simeon seven thousand one hundred, while remote Zebulun brought fifty thousand, Asher forty thousand, and the two tribes and a half beyond Jordan a hundred and twenty thousand. Not that the adjacent tribes were cold in the cause: they showed as much prudence in bringing few, all the rest lying so near within call, as the others showed zeal in bringing many — and the men of Judah, he adds, had enough to do entertaining those who came from afar.
25:
Simeon's seven thousand one hundred are described as mighty men of valour for the war. Ellicott would render the last words rather as "for warfare," or military service — the same correction he makes to the description of Judah's contingent in the verse before, which he translates "equipped for warfare."

Levi's four thousand six hundred draw the longer note, since a tribe of priests mustering for battle wants explaining. Ellicott begins with the grammar: the Hebrew reads "of the sons of the Levite," and the article shows that the name is gentilic or tribal here rather than personal. Then he supplies the comparison that makes the thing intelligible — these martial Levites remind us of the priestly warriors of the crusades — and he points out that Levites might be soldiers, and in fact must have been such for the defence of the sanctuaries, as the chronicler's own notices of the men of valour among the gatekeepers show (1 Chronicles 9:13; 1 Chronicles 9:19; 2 Chronicles 23:1).

Henry reads their presence as a matter of conviction rather than of arms. The Levites themselves and the priests, called here the Aaronites, appeared very hearty in this cause, and were ready, if there were occasion, to fight for David as well as pray for him, because they knew he was called of God to the government.

One question the figure leaves open Ellicott raises at once: it is not clear whether the three thousand seven hundred who come with Jehoiada in the next verse are included in this four thousand six hundred or counted beside it, and he judges that probably they are not. Keil and Delitzsch pass straight from the totals to the names, treating the verses that follow as the roll of the Aaronite leaders rather than as a second reckoning of the tribe.

Henry notices how the register varies its praise. Of most of these contingents it is said that they were mighty men of valour, of others that they were expert in war, and of them all that they could keep rank: they had a great deal of martial fire, he says, and yet were governable and subject to the rules of order — warm hearts but cool heads. Some were considerate enough, he adds, to bring arms and all instruments for war along with them, since they could hardly suppose David able to furnish them.
27:
The one point urged on every side here is a negative: Jehoiada was not the high priest. Ellicott renders the phrase literally, "Jehoiada the prince belonging to Aaron," the noun being that used elsewhere of a chief officer (1 Chronicles 9:11; 1 Chronicles 9:20), while "Aaron" stands for the leading clan of Levi rather than for the man. His post was accordingly military — head of the warriors of his own kindred — since the pontificate at that date belonged to Abiathar (1 Samuel 23:9). Keil and Delitzsch mark the boundary in Latin: prince of the house of Aaron and chief of the Aaronite family he was, but not princeps sacerdotum, a style reserved for the sacerdotal office another then occupied. Clarke compresses both halves into a line, making Jehoiada captain over the warriors of Aaron's house. Wesley calls him simply a man of eminent place serving under the high priest (1 Samuel 23:6). The three thousand seven hundred who came with him are, on this reading, the fighting strength of the clan he headed.

Who he was apart from that office stays a conjecture. Rashi, Kimchi and others, as Keil and Delitzsch report them, identified him with the father of Benaiah; Ellicott arrives at the same guess, pointing to the Benaiah of the roll of heroes (1 Chronicles 11:22).

Zadok enters as a youth, and his identity is handled with equal reserve. Ellicott's version runs "And Zadok, a youth, a valiant warrior," and he wonders whether this is the man who afterwards succeeded Abiathar (1 Kings 2:26; 1 Kings 4:4); Keil and Delitzsch allow the same possibility, stressing that he was still a lad at the time of this muster.

The twenty-two princes attached to him measure the strength of a single family. Ellicott reads the clause as "his father-house, princes twenty and two," and infers that the sub-clan of Eleazar must have been populous indeed to yield so many captains, with the companies of warriors implied behind them. Keil and Delitzsch trace the same descent from Eleazar and have the twenty-two chiefs travel south in Zadok's company. What no part of the register supplies, Ellicott remarks, is a grand total for Levi; and he would omit the two supplied verbs the Authorised Version prints across these verses.
29:
Benjamin's three thousand is a small figure beside the rest, and the register itself explains why. Ellicott glosses "kindred" as fellow-tribesmen and "hitherto" as up to that time (1 Chronicles 9:18), and reads the clause that follows as a continuing action — they were still keeping guard over the house of Saul (Numbers 3:38). Both that clause and the phrase about Saul's fellow-tribesmen, he says, stand there to account for the smallness of the Benjamite muster; and the tribe's reluctance to recognise David survived the murder of Ish-bosheth. Keil and Delitzsch take the verse the same way: the greater number of the Benjamites were devoted to the interests of the fallen house, and from this we learn that their attachment to Saul outlasted his son's death and that they could bring themselves to acknowledge David only with difficulty (Genesis 26:5; Leviticus 8:35). Wesley puts the motive bluntly: they endeavoured to keep the crown in Saul's family.

Henry judges them more sharply. Some of Saul's kindred did come over, though not so many as from the other tribes, because a foolish affection for their own tribe and a jealousy for its honour kept many of them long in the sinking interest of Saul's family. Kindred, he says, should never over-rule conscience; call no man father to that extent but God only.

Ephraim's twenty thousand eight hundred brings a phrase to settle. "Famous throughout the house of their fathers" Ellicott would render as men of name, that is of renown, an expression he traces to Genesis 6:4, with the men arranged according to their clans; Keil and Delitzsch send the reader to the same verse for the idiom and take the last words as "in their fathers'-houses." The title, Ellicott adds, is a natural addition to "valiant heroes" and need occasion no surprise, their renown being doubtless collective rather than individual.

The size of that company Ellicott finds noticeable for its smallness, and he offers two accounts of it without choosing between them: either the tribe was already in decline within the Mosaic period, as the two censuses may suggest (Numbers 1:33; Numbers 26:37), or it had been greatly reduced by Saul's last wars with the Philistines (2 Samuel 2:9).
31:
Half Manasseh's eighteen thousand are marked by how they were chosen. Ellicott translates "expressed by name" as pricked down, or entered in a list, by names (1 Chronicles 16:41; Numbers 1:17), the men having been levied by the tribal chiefs and enrolled for this service. Keil and Delitzsch press a further inference out of the phrase: the tribe must have held a general consultation and determined on sending representatives, chosen as famous men to go and make David king. Wesley takes the detail devotionally — these were men not ashamed publicly to own David by putting their names to a paper — and notes, as Keil and Delitzsch do, that the half tribe meant is the one within Jordan, the other being spoken of later.

Issachar's two hundred provoke the longest argument in the chapter, and it turns on what "understanding of the times" means. Clarke gives the Targum, which makes them astronomers and astrologers: skilled in fixing the beginnings of years, the commencement of months and the intercalation of months and years, in the changes of the moon, and astrologers in signs and stars, that they might show Israel what to do — their brethren excelling in the words of the law and obedient to their command. Keil and Delitzsch report the same conclusion from the older commentators, the Targum and various rabbins among them, that the tribe had distinguished itself beyond the others in astronomical and physical knowledge; Ellicott reports it of the old Jewish expositors, who held that Issachar read in the heavens which seasons were auspicious for action, as the ancient Babylonians professed to do.

Both then refuse it. The words, Keil and Delitzsch say, do not suggest astronomical or astrological knowledge but merely state that these men knew the times for every matter and every business — a reading they take from Salomo ben-Melech's Miclol Yophi, who set beside it the wise man's word that each thing has its own time and opportunity (Ecclesiastes 3:1). Ellicott is blunter: all the text really asserts is that the men who went over to David thereby showed political sagacity, and no similar phrase occurs elsewhere in the Old Testament. His own rendering runs "men sage in discernment for the times," the times being critical junctures.

Henry keeps three possibilities open and then chooses. They may have understood the natural times, discerning the face of the sky and advising their neighbours on the seasons for ploughing, sowing and reaping; or the ceremonial times appointed for the solemn feasts, which is why they are said to call the people to the mountain (Deuteronomy 33:19), almanacs not then being as common as now; or, rather, the political times — for it is the periphrasis of statesmen that they know the times (Esther 1:13). Wesley settles on that last sense and offers a demonstration: Issachar adhered to Saul while he lived, knowing the time was not yet come for David to take the kingdom, and could not join David while Abner lived and commanded the tribes that encircled them, but owned him as king as soon as Abner was dead and they had opportunity to declare themselves.

Whether the praise belongs to the tribe or to its chiefs is a smaller question. Keil and Delitzsch restrict it to the two hundred heads, whom Lavater calls prudent men; Ellicott has the clansmen march at their chieftains' mouth (Numbers 4:27) and observes that Issachar's total is never given. Henry, counting them the fewest of all, makes the two hundred in effect the whole tribe, as serviceable to David's interest as those who brought the greatest numbers: the commonality having bowed their shoulder to bear (Genesis 49:15), the great men had them at their beck — they knew how to rule and the rest knew how to obey.
33:
Zebulun's fifty thousand come with the fullest description in the list, and one word in it is a genuine puzzle. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the opening phrase as practice in the use of all kinds of weapons for war; Ellicott translates it "marshalling battle with all kinds of weapons of war." What follows, rendered in the Authorised Version as "which could keep rank," rests on a verb occurring nowhere else but here and at the close of the chapter.

Two readings compete for it. The Greek and the Latin both translate "to help," and nine manuscripts carry the Hebrew word for helping rather than the word in the text. Ellicott records this, and Keil and Delitzsch admit they would be inclined to take the rarer form as an Aramaic equivalent of the ordinary verb to help, were it not for its second occurrence; there the connection demands the sense "to close up together," to set the battle array in order, and so they read it here as well. Ellicott reaches the same translation, "falling into rank," or forming in line. The Syriac, he notes, leaves the word aside and paraphrases: to make war with those who disputed the sovereignty of David.

"Not of double heart" is the clause each of them wants. Ellicott gives the Hebrew idiom literally — without a heart and a heart — and sets beside it the psalmist's speech of smooth things spoken with heart and heart, by men who think one thing and say another (Psalms 12:3); the phrase asserts the unwavering fidelity and resolute courage of these warriors. Wesley says as much in plainer words: they were sincerely loyal and did not dissemble with David, pretending to be for him while in their hearts they favoured Saul's family, and none had any separate interests but all were for the public good. Henry singles the tribe out for it — of all the contingents these are the ones said to be not of double heart, and in this matter they were Israelites indeed, in whom was no guile.

The size of the contingent has been thought surprising. Ellicott reports the objection that Zebulun and Naphtali never played an important part in the history of Israel, answers it with a single cross-reference (Judges 5:18), and adds that the figures here are at all events not discordant with those of the wilderness censuses (Numbers 1:31; Numbers 26:27).

Naphtali follows with a thousand captains and thirty-seven thousand men bearing shield and spear, and the word for spear here, Ellicott observes, is not the one used of the men of Judah who "bare shield and spear" earlier in the muster. The English covers two Hebrew nouns, and the weapons they name may have differed in use: perhaps the one was thrown and the other thrust. Keil and Delitzsch make no separate comment on the tribe, carrying their exposition straight on through the remaining contingents to the subscription that closes the list.
35:
Dan is given a single clause, and the first thing Ellicott notes about it is grammatical. The Hebrew reads "the Danite," in the singular, exactly as Levi had been "the Levite" — the article making the name tribal rather than personal. Having elsewhere had to account for Dan's absence from the chronicler's genealogies, he remarks with some satisfaction that the tribe is not omitted from the present list.

Asher's forty thousand are "such as went forth to battle, expert in war," and Ellicott takes the last words literally as to order or marshal battle — the very phrase that has already described Zebulun and Dan. He judges the margin's rendering, "rangers of battle," a good one.

The hundred and twenty thousand from beyond Jordan close the muster, and Ellicott would correct the preposition: better "from the other side," that is, from Peraea, since these men came across rather than stayed there. Their equipment he renders as all kinds of weapons of warlike service. The figure itself he calls certainly remarkable for two and a half tribes, and then declines to pursue it: admitting that the ciphers here and elsewhere may be corrupt, the want of other documents against which the text might be compared renders further criticism superfluous.
38:
Ellicott marks this verse as the conclusion of the list and re-translates it: "All the above, being men of war, forming line of battle with whole heart, came to Hebron to make David king." The phrase he renders "forming line of battle" is the rare verb from Zebulun's clause, here given its proper object; and he would move the pause in the sentence, since the Hebrew seems to stop at "line of battle" where it reads better after "with whole heart" — literally, with a heart entire, so that they formed in line with fearless intrepidity. Gill's gloss on "could keep rank" is simply that they were well disciplined men.

"All the rest also of Israel" covers those who did not appear at Hebron in person. The word for the rest, Ellicott notes, is used nowhere else, and the Hebrew says that the remainder of Israel was one heart, that is, unanimous (2 Chronicles 30:12). Henry takes those two phrases for the point of the whole muster: these men engaged in the enterprise with a perfect heart, and their perfection lay in being of one heart.

How many were there is where the arithmetic and the criticism meet. Allowing an average for Issachar, whose total the list never gives, Ellicott puts the warriors assembled at upwards of three hundred thousand, and argues that the figure should not surprise us: in those days every able-bodied man was as a matter of course trained in the use of arms and liable to be called out for the king's wars, so that "man" and "warrior" were almost convertible terms. Nor was this a parade of the nation's entire strength, as the six hundred thousand of the Exodus and the one million three hundred thousand of David's census show.

On the proportions between the tribes Ellicott is candid and then sharp. The suggestions he has offered along the way are uncertain, the fact being that we do not know enough of the condition of the tribes at that epoch to pronounce on the relative probability of the numbers assigned them. But that candour is just why he refuses Reuss's verdict — that it is absolutely inconceivable the nearer tribes, Judah above all, should have furnished so small a contingent while the figures rise in direct proportion to the distance travelled — calling it a hasty and uncritical exaggeration.

The three days that follow are a festival. Gill says they kept it to testify their joy on the occasion; Keil and Delitzsch call them festive meals, held because their brethren had prepared the provisions (1 Samuel 30:16; 1 Kings 1:45). Clarke doubts the whole host can have sat down to it — it is not possible that all the thousands named above feasted with David for three days, so these must be the deputies of the different peoples — and yet even of these there was a great number, since the men of Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali, nearest to this place of rendezvous, had brought all the necessaries for such a feast. From the whole, Clarke concludes, it is most evident that the great majority of the tribes wished to see the kingdom confirmed in David's hands; nor was there ever in any country a man more worthy of the public choice, since as statesman, warrior, hero, poet and divine he stands unrivalled in the annals of the world.
40:
Who sent the provisions is read a little more widely than the verse at first suggests. Gill takes "they that were nigh" for those near Hebron, or bordering on the tribe of Judah. Ellicott grants that the tribes bordering Judah contributed, the Greek rendering the phrase as the neighbouring peoples, but adds that the northern tribes did so as well. Keil and Delitzsch spell the point out: it was not these alone who performed the service but also those of the remaining tribes dwelling near them, so that the men of Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali on the northern frontier of Canaan, as well as those who bordered upon Judah, sent provisions on beasts of burden.

The beasts and the food both draw comment. Ellicott notices which animals are listed and which is not: asses, camels, mules and oxen were the usual beasts of burden in rocky Canaan, but not horses. "Meat, meal" he would render food of flour, and "bunches" he corrects to cakes of raisins, masses of dried figs and raisins having been, and remaining, a staple article of food in the East (1 Samuel 25:18; Amos 8:11). Keil and Delitzsch gloss the same two Hebrew words as masses of dried figs and masses of raisins or cakes, and send the reader to the same place in Samuel for them. The simple diction of the narrative, Ellicott adds, puts him in mind of Homer's feasts and is a mark of its ancient origin.

Why the provisions came is the clause the grammarians and the preachers alike settle on: "for there was joy in Israel." Keil and Delitzsch make it the motive — this joy moved those who remained at home to show their sympathy with the national festival solemnized at Hebron by sending the provisions. Henry reads it as a proper proportion between labour and charge: those who were at the least pains in travelling to this convention, or congress of states, thought themselves obliged to be at so much the more charge in entertaining the rest, that there might be something of an equality. A noble feast was made on the occasion, he says — a feast made for laughter (Ecclesiastes 10:19) — and with good reason, for when the righteous bear rule the city rejoices.

Henry then turns the three days into an argument. When the throne of Christ is set up in a soul there is, or ought to be, great joy in that soul, and provision is made for its feasting, not as here for two or three days but for the whole life and for eternity. Happy are those, he closes, who wisely perceive it their duty and interest to submit to the Saviour Jesus Christ, the Son of David, renouncing for his sake all that is inconsistent with him, and whose earnest endeavours to do good are directed by the wisdom God gives through acquaintance with his word, experience and observation — and if any man lack that wisdom, let him ask it of God, who gives to all men liberally and upbraids not.

Ellicott ends his notes on the chapter by looking forward, marking the chapters that follow as a complete section on the transfer of the ark from Kirjath-jearim to its new sanctuary at Jerusalem, a narrative closely parallel to the account in Samuel (2 Samuel 6:1).
